review_notes.justification: The qualification accepts that RLHF has a structural flaw but relocates it from the human annotator to the costless reward signal.
The qualification accepts calibration as useful while holding that it cannot supply its own reference where no answer key exists.
The qualification accepts that closed-choice outputs cannot fabricate text while denying that this eliminates error.
The extension applies the limits of internal monitoring loops to calibrated decision engines and adds a cost for careless checking.
The extension places decentralized validation of feedback as the third layer of a stack alongside verifiable rewards and calibrated decisions.
The extension applies the migration of the binding constraint from generation to evaluation to the question of what succeeds RLHF.

positions.text: TypeSafe's case for Jev locates RLHF's flaw in the human in the loop. Kaal's position is that the flaw is institutional: whoever supplies the reward signal bears no consequence for being wrong. A model that labels in the annotator's place loses nothing either. Replacing the human does not fix it; giving the signal a price does.
scope_conditions: TypeSafe's post announces a product. It is not an empirical test of these claims.
The position is Kaal's own argument in the essay After RLHF Comes a Stack, Not a Model.
The position does not evaluate Jev's accuracy, which TypeSafe has not published a calibration figure for.
The accountable-validation layer is proposed, not tested: no policy has yet been trained under it.

positions.text: Calibration is a property of populations, not of single decisions. A model can be calibrated on average and miscalibrated on a subgroup, and it can drift. Someone has to keep checking it on cases it has never seen, from outside its own data loop, and must bear a cost for checking carelessly.
